$comment: Rules about the inputs an analysis must establish before it can conclude anything: what the money is for, when it is needed, what must stay reachable, what is held back against emergencies, and what is owed. Standards 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6. These five come first in the series because every later judgement — about risk, concentration, scenarios — is a judgement relative to them, and a document that never states them has not been cautious, it has been unanchored.
$admissionTest: Five of these fifteen are `manual-review` with `assurance: none`, and each earned its place under all five questions in ADR 0005 rather than in spite of them: a reviewer can gather the evidence, evaluate it, explain the violation, and remediate it. The requirements that failed the test are named in each standard's Implementation section and stay in prose — Standard 3's blended horizon, Standard 4's realised-loss framing, Standard 5's opportunity-cost rhetoric, Standard 6's undisclosed outstanding borrowing. Those are disclosed gaps, not silent ones.

rules.title: A planning or recommendation document states the objective it serves
rules.description: A document operating in planning or personalized-recommendation mode states the objective it serves, in the document, before the analysis that rests on it.
rules.rationale: Every later judgement in this series is conditional on the objective — whether the horizon suits the risk, whether the drawdown schedule is met, whether a shortfall is survivable. Without one on the page the conclusions are true of nobody in particular, and neither the reader nor a reviewer can tell whether the analysis was addressed to them.
rules.remediation: State the objective before the analysis, in terms the reader recognises as their own situation rather than as a category. Where it is genuinely unknown, mark it [requires personal financial context] and present the work as analysis rather than as a plan.
rules.$assuranceNote: Lexical, and it applies only to documents that declare a planning or recommendation mode — so a document that mislabels its mode escapes it entirely. It establishes that an objective statement is PRESENT and sits before the analysis. It never establishes that the objective is the reader's ACTUAL one, nor that it is well chosen. A document that invents a plausible objective passes cleanly.

rules.title: A stated objective carries an amount and a date
rules.description: The stated objective specifies how much is required and when it is required, or marks either as unknown under Standard 27 rather than omitting it.
rules.rationale: "Growth" names a direction and no destination, and an objective that cannot be failed guarantees that every analysis conducted against it returns a favourable answer. The amount and the date are what turn an aspiration into something a projection can miss.
rules.remediation: Add the sum required and the date it is required by, and state the consequence of missing it alongside. Where one element is unknown, mark it rather than dropping it.
rules.$assuranceNote: Lexical: it looks for a monetary quantity and a date near the objective statement. It establishes SHAPE and never CORRECTNESS or ADEQUACY — "objective: growth, by 2040, £100,000" satisfies the check while failing the requirement in substance. The consequence-of-failure element the standard also demands is not reachable by any pattern this repository can run, and its absence is disclosed rather than counted as a pass.

rules.title: Competing objectives are ranked, and which gives way first is stated
rules.description: Where a document serves more than one objective it states their order of precedence and states which is sacrificed first when they conflict.
rules.rationale: Objectives compete for the same money and the competition is invisible in the output: a single allocation serving both a near-term deposit and a long-term retirement has already answered a weighting question the document never asked. Stating the ranking is the only thing that makes that trade-off contestable, and contestable is the only way it gets corrected.
rules.remediation: List the objectives in precedence order, state explicitly which is sacrificed first, and show that the allocation reflects that order rather than an average of them.
rules.$assuranceNote: Reports NOT_EVALUATED until a person records a judgement, and no automated check can close that gap. Recovering the weighting a document applied means reading the analysis and forming a view about what it optimised; the allocation looks identical whether the ranking was deliberate, accidental, or absent, so there is no textual artefact to find. Searching for the word "priority" would confirm that the word was used and nothing else.

rules.title: A statement about risk names the horizon it is relative to
rules.description: A document that characterises risk — as high, low, suitable, acceptable, or conservative — states the time horizon that characterisation is relative to.
rules.rationale: The same volatility is tolerable over thirty years and reckless over three. A risk level stated without a horizon is a number with no unit, and the reader supplies the missing unit themselves, usually the one that makes the recommendation look reasonable.
rules.remediation: State the horizon beside the risk characterisation. Where several horizons apply, state each and analyse them separately rather than blending them into an average.
rules.$assuranceNote: Lexical. It establishes that a horizon is PRESENT somewhere near risk language — never that it is the reader's real horizon, and never that the analysis respected it. A document stating a four-year horizon and then projecting to thirty passes this check and trips nothing else automatically.

rules.title: The projection horizon agrees with the date the objective states
rules.description: The horizon used in a projection matches the date the money is needed as stated in the document's objective section, rather than the date the analysis happens to end.
rules.rationale: An analysis that ends where the model is convenient rather than where the money is needed answers a question nobody asked, and the substitution is invisible once the two dates sit on different pages. Ending late flatters the result by exactly the compounding the reader will not get.
rules.remediation: Set the projection horizon to the objective's date. Where they must differ, state why and show what the difference does to the conclusion.
rules.$assuranceNote: It compares two dates the document itself states, so it establishes that the two figures AGREE and nothing more. It never establishes that either date is CORRECT: two matching dates that are both wrong pass, and so does a document whose objective section was written to match a horizon already chosen for other reasons.

rules.title: A short horizon constrains the allocation rather than being disclosed beside it
rules.description: Where the horizon is short, the recommended allocation is actually limited by it, rather than the horizon being noted alongside an allocation chosen on other grounds.
rules.rationale: Disclosure and constraint are different acts. An allocation that would be wrong for a three-year horizon does not become right because the document mentions the three years, and the annotated form is the one that reads as compliance while changing nothing.
rules.remediation: Show the constraint operating: state the maximum risk the horizon permits, then derive the allocation from that bound, rather than annotating an allocation that was already settled.
rules.$assuranceNote: Reports NOT_EVALUATED until a person records a judgement. The compliant document and the merely annotated one contain the same two elements — a horizon and an allocation — and differ only in whether the first determined the second. That is a fact about how the analysis was conducted, not about what the document says, and nothing in the text distinguishes them.

rules.title: An allocation states the liquidity it requires before the return it expects
rules.description: A document producing an allocation states the cash the holder will need and when, before it states the return the allocation is expected to produce.
rules.rationale: A higher-returning allocation that must be sold at the wrong moment returns less than a lower-returning one that need not be. Stating the requirement first is what stops it being treated as a residual the return figure can bargain against.
rules.remediation: State the amounts required and their timing at the head of the allocation section, and show that the allocation meets them before any expected return is compared.
rules.$assuranceNote: Lexical and positional. It establishes that a liquidity statement is PRESENT and precedes the return figures — never that the requirements listed are COMPLETE or true. A document listing "liquidity needs: none" satisfies this check entirely, and nothing available to this repository can contradict it.

rules.title: Notice periods and redemption restrictions are stated where they exist
rules.description: A document recommending an instrument that carries a notice period, redemption window, gating provision, or exit penalty states those terms at the point of recommendation.
rules.rationale: The terms governing how money comes back out matter only in the circumstances where they are hardest to discover, and an instrument's illiquidity is the property least salient at the moment it is bought. Disclosed late, the terms are news; disclosed at the recommendation, they are a decision input.
rules.remediation: Name the notice period, the redemption frequency, any gating or suspension provision, and any exit charge, beside the recommendation rather than in an appendix.
rules.$assuranceNote: Lexical. It establishes that terms are DESCRIBED near the instrument, never that the description is ACCURATE or complete. A stated 30-day notice period on an instrument whose documentation also permits suspension passes, and no scan available here reads the instrument's documentation. It also cannot detect the restriction an author never mentioned.

rules.title: Required liquidity enters the analysis as a constraint, not as an adjustable input
rules.description: The liquidity the holder requires is treated as a bound the allocation must satisfy, rather than as a term that expected return was permitted to outbid.
rules.rationale: Once required liquidity becomes one term in an objective function, a sufficiently attractive return will always buy it out — and the trade the optimisation made is not visible in the allocation it produced. Liquidity is a constraint, not a preference, and the difference is structural rather than rhetorical.
rules.remediation: State the liquidity requirement as a constraint, show the feasible set it leaves, and select within that set. Never present a return advantage as grounds for reducing the requirement.
rules.$assuranceNote: Reports NOT_EVALUATED until a person records a judgement. How an optimisation was formulated is usually not in the document at all — the output is an allocation, and a constrained and an unconstrained formulation can return the same one. No check can recover the formulation from its result, so no check can tell a satisfied constraint from a bought-out preference.

rules.title: A reserve is sized in months of essential expenses
rules.description: A document stating an emergency reserve expresses it as a number of months of essential expenses, rather than as a share of assets or as a round sum.
rules.rationale: A reserve exists to cover expenses for a period without income, so expenses and time are its natural units. A percentage of assets sizes the reserve to the portfolio, which is the quantity least related to what the reserve is actually for, and it shrinks the reserve in precisely the markets that trigger the emergency.
rules.remediation: State the monthly essential expense figure and the number of months covered, and derive the amount from the two rather than the other way round.
rules.$assuranceNote: Lexical: it establishes that the reserve is EXPRESSED in months of expenses. It cannot establish that the expense figure is right, that the number of months is adequate, or that the named instrument actually releases the money in time — "6 months, held in a stocks and shares ISA" passes this check cleanly.

rules.title: The instruments holding the reserve are named with their access terms
rules.description: The document names where the reserve is held and states how quickly those instruments release funds, including any notice period, settlement delay, or early-access penalty.
rules.rationale: A reserve that cannot be reached inside the window an emergency allows is not a reserve; it is an investment wearing an optimistic label. The access terms are the whole of the difference between the two, and they are the part most often left unstated.
rules.remediation: Name each instrument holding the reserve and state its settlement or notice period and any penalty, measured against the time the emergencies it is for would actually allow.
rules.$assuranceNote: Lexical. It establishes that access terms are STATED, never that they are correct and never that the stated speed is adequate to any particular emergency. A document asserting "instantly accessible" of a fund that settles at T+3 passes, and nothing here checks the claim against the instrument.

rules.title: The number of months is justified against the holder's actual circumstances
rules.description: The document connects the number of months it states to the personal factors that determine it — income stability, dependants, insurance cover, notice period, health, and the cost of the likely emergencies — rather than citing a conventional figure.
rules.rationale: There is no universal adequate number of months, and a general figure repeated as though there were is this standard's central failure. The reserve a single earner with variable income needs is not the reserve two salaried earners need, and the conventional answer is wrong for both in different directions.
rules.remediation: State the factors that set the number for this holder and show which way each moves it. Where a factor is unknown, mark it rather than defaulting to a conventional figure.
rules.$assuranceNote: Reports NOT_EVALUATED until a person records a judgement. Whether the factors a document cites actually support the number of months it states is the central judgement of Standard 5, and answering it requires the holder's circumstances, which are outside the document by construction. A document can recite exactly the right factors and still state a number unrelated to any of them, and the two are textually indistinguishable.

rules.title: A stated periodic payment is accompanied by the total cost of borrowing
rules.description: A document presenting a periodic loan payment also states the total interest paid over the full term.
rules.rationale: A monthly payment is the figure chosen for how affordable it reads, and it says nothing about what the borrowing costs. The lifetime total is what makes a long term with a low payment comparable to a short one, and without it lengthening the term looks like a saving.
rules.remediation: State total interest over the term beside the payment, and carry the arithmetic in a calc block so the figure can be recomputed rather than trusted.
rules.$assuranceNote: Lexical: it establishes that a lifetime-total figure is PRESENT beside the payment, never that it is CORRECT. A total computed on the wrong rate or the wrong term passes. Where the document carries the arithmetic in a calc block, math.calc-blocks-recompute checks the arithmetic exactly — but full assurance over the arithmetic is not assurance over the analysis.

rules.title: A document raising borrowing to invest carries an adverse scenario
rules.description: Where a document raises borrowing to invest, it contains an adverse scenario section addressing the leveraged downside, including the point at which the position must be closed.
rules.rationale: Leverage multiplies losses as well as gains and adds a failure mode the unleveraged case does not have: being forced to sell at the worst moment. Presenting the expected spread without that case is an argument rather than an analysis, and the asymmetry is the entire subject.
rules.remediation: Model the leveraged adverse case with the cost of borrowing and the forced-close threshold, and present it before the expected spread rather than after it.
rules.$assuranceNote: Structural: it establishes that an adverse section is PRESENT in a document that mentions leverage, never that the section is ADEQUATE. An adverse case describing a 5% decline passes while failing the requirement in every way that matters, and the ordering the standard demands — adverse case before expected spread — is not checked here at all.

rules.title: Repaying debt and investing are compared on a like-for-like basis
rules.description: A comparison between repaying debt and investing puts the two on the same footing: the same horizon, the same tax treatment, and a certain return on repayment set against an uncertain one on investment.
rules.rationale: Debt repayment returns the interest rate with certainty; investing returns an expectation. Comparing the two headline numbers without pricing that difference systematically favours investing — which is also, not coincidentally, the more profitable recommendation.
rules.remediation: State both sides net of tax over the same horizon, mark the repayment return as certain and the investment return as a distribution, and say what the comparison assumes about risk.
rules.$assuranceNote: Reports NOT_EVALUATED until a person records a judgement. Whether two figures were computed on the same basis is a fact about how they were derived, and the derivations are almost never in the document; two numbers set side by side look comparable whether or not they are, and a checker sees only the pair.
